title: When Being Hindu in America Feels Unsafe, California's Answer Is a Room Full of Cops and Community Leaders
excerpt: The Coalition of Hindus of North America partnered with San Jose Police and the Santa Clara DA to launch Suraksha — a safety initiative born of rising Hinduphobia across the United States
body:
The event was called Suraksha — the Hindi word for protection. On a recent weekend in San Jose, California, the Coalition of Hindus of North America (CoHNA) brought together an unlikely assembly: Hindu community leaders, uniformed officers from the San Jose Police Department, and prosecutors from the Santa Clara County District Attorney's office. Their shared agenda was as simple as it was sobering — teaching Hindu Americans how to report hate crimes, and training law enforcement to recognise them.

The need for such an event tells its own story. Across the United States, Hinduphobia has escalated from fringe online abuse to a pattern of real-world violence and intimidation that has left many in the diaspora feeling vulnerable. Temples in California have been vandalised. Graffiti bearing pro-Khalistan slogans has appeared on Hindu places of worship. Families report harassment and threats that often go unreported because victims do not know how — or whether it is worth the effort — to engage with law enforcement.

## A trust deficit, decades in the making

For many first-generation Indian immigrants, the instinct to avoid involving the police runs deep. In India, interactions with law enforcement are rarely pleasant; the default posture is avoidance. That cultural reflex has followed the diaspora to America, where under-reporting of hate crimes means the true scale of anti-Hindu hostility remains invisible in official statistics.

Suraksha was designed to bridge precisely this gap. CoHNA's programme included sessions on how hate crimes are defined under California law, the step-by-step process for filing a report, and what victims can expect from the district attorney's office once a case moves forward. San Jose Police officers explained how their department's hate crimes unit operates, emphasising that every report matters — even those that do not lead to immediate arrests — because documented patterns of hostility help unlock federal resources and policy responses.

"The single biggest barrier is awareness," said a CoHNA spokesperson at the event. "People don't know that vandalising a temple or shouting slurs at someone because of their faith is a prosecutable hate crime in California. We're here to change that."

## The numbers that matter

California tracks hate crimes more rigorously than most American states, but the data still lags behind lived experience. The state recorded over 3.1 million hate-related acts in the most recent reporting period — a number that encompasses everything from verbal abuse to physical violence. South Asian communities, including Hindus, Sikhs, and Muslims, have each faced distinct but overlapping forms of targeting. Hindu temples have been burgled and defaced. Students have been bullied. Professionals have faced workplace discrimination that often flies under the radar of HR departments trained to recognise other forms of bias.

For the Hindu diaspora, the pattern is particularly disorienting because it comes at a moment of unprecedented visibility and success in American public life. Indian Americans occupy senior positions in technology, finance, medicine, and government. Yet this prominence has done little to insulate ordinary community members from hostility — and may, paradoxically, have made them more visible targets.

## What Suraksha signals for the wider diaspora

The San Jose initiative is significant beyond its immediate locality. It represents a shift in how Hindu American organisations engage with the state. Historically, diaspora groups have focused their advocacy on issues in India — temple restorations, political developments in their home states, or fundraising for natural disasters. Suraksha marks a pivot toward a distinctly American form of civic engagement: building institutional relationships with local law enforcement, demanding accountability from district attorneys, and ensuring that anti-Hindu bias is treated with the same seriousness as other forms of hate.

The model is not new. Jewish, Black, Muslim, and LGBTQ communities in the United States have long maintained formal liaisons with police departments and prosecutors' offices. Hindu organisations are now following that playbook, recognising that political influence in Washington means little if community members in San Jose, Houston, or Atlanta feel unsafe walking to their local mandir.

## The road ahead

CoHNA has signalled that Suraksha is not a one-off event but the beginning of a national programme. Plans are under way to replicate the format in other cities with large Hindu populations, including Houston, Chicago, and the Washington, D.C. suburbs of northern Virginia. The organisation is also lobbying for the FBI's hate crime reporting system to adopt more granular categories for South Asian communities, arguing that the current taxonomy obscures the specific nature of anti-Hindu hostility.

For NRIs who left India seeking security and opportunity, the irony is hard to miss. The country that promised freedom of worship now requires a formal safety initiative to protect the faithful. Suraksha may be a Hindi word, but the problem it addresses is entirely American.
